QF.id: XIII Introduction to the Underlying Markets_75

question.text: What is the significance of the 'repo rate' set by RBI, and how does it connect all three underlying markets?

answer.text: The repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends to banks — it influences short-term money market rates, bond yields (through the yield curve), equity valuations (through discount rates), and currency rates (through interest rate differentials)
The repo rate only affects the banking sector and has no impact on equity or currency markets
The repo rate determines the exact price of all government bonds
The repo rate is set by SEBI and applies only to derivative margin calculations

explanation.text: The Logic: The repo rate is RBI's main policy lending rate to banks, and it operates as the anchor of India's interest rate environment. It transmits to short-term money market rates almost directly, influences the entire G-Sec yield curve and bond prices through expectations, feeds into equity valuations via the discount rate applied in DCF and earnings-yield comparisons, and affects currency markets through cross-country interest rate differentials and covered interest parity. The Trap: The repo rate is not "banking only" — its impact reaches well beyond banks into bonds, equities, and currencies. It does not mechanically fix bond prices; it influences them through expectations and the yield curve. And it is set by RBI's MPC, not by SEBI. Note: The full three-market linkage as worded — particularly the equity valuation/discount-rate channel — was not located across the cited workbook pages (IR p.15, p.30, p.99; Currency p.32). The framing above is general monetary-policy transmission knowledge, not a workbook citation; only the repo-to-money-market and repo-to-bond-yield channels are directly traceable to the cited sources.
